rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. Use a midrange temperature so subsequent runs can probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the critical pair responds to reduced steepness. The modest increase should keep the last peak near or below 10 minutes while potentially improving its resolution.
The critical pair improves with a shallower gradient, but further lengthening risks the time penalty. Raise temperature by 5 C to test selectivity while creating additional time margin.

The critical pair converged sharply at 45 C; testing 55 C may separate it again after an elution-order reversal. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate this selectivity effect while shortening retention.

Shorten the gradient at 55 C: after the apparent elution-order reversal, increasing steepness may widen the critical pair rather than compress it. This also reduces run time, while the other pairs have useful resolution margins.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a shorter gradient to seek the same full resolution in less time. The pair at R 1.59 is the likely limiting pair, so retain injection 5 as the benchmark if it deteriorates.

Use a narrower window with the same gradient slope as the fully resolved injection 5, but a higher starting organic fraction to shorten retention. This tests whether full resolution can be preserved without the excessive steepness of injection 6.

Explore a faster, hotter regime that may reverse and then separate the newly limiting pair, while improving the previously critical pair. Injection 5 remains the maximum-score fallback if this selectivity change leaves any pair unresolved.

Raise the starting organic fraction to test whether the limiting pair separates further after its apparent order reversal at 60 C. The slightly narrower gradient moderates compression while targeting a fully resolved run shorter than injection 5.

Increase the starting organic fraction another step to improve the remaining critical pair, while reducing the slope slightly to protect its neighboring pair. Monitor the earliest pair for compression as retention decreases.

Explore the low-temperature selectivity branch with a fast gradient, retaining injection 5 as the maximum-score benchmark. Lowering the starting organic fraction protects the early peaks, while the temperature change may resolve the central cluster in a different order.

Return to 40 C with a shallower gradient to improve the critical pair identified in injections 1–2. A higher starting organic fraction should offset the added retention time while keeping the early peaks retained, potentially providing a second fully resolved method.

Refine the successful 55 C regime with a shallower, narrower gradient to recover the pair that deteriorated in injection 7. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset the slower slope and may preserve full resolution with a slightly earlier last peak than injection 5.

Refine near the fully resolved method with a modestly higher starting fraction and a shallower slope. This should recover the limiting pair from injection 7 while retaining the improved separation of its other critical pair, potentially matching the maximum CRF with similar retention time.

Test a steeper gradient on the reversed-order branch at 60 C to increase separation of the limiting pair. Use a moderate starting fraction to protect the earliest peaks and assess whether the neighboring central pair still has sufficient resolution.

Return to the near-optimal injection 14 and reduce the slope one grid step to lift its R 1.47 pair above baseline resolution. This targets a second maximum-score method with improved resolution margins, while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test a 5 C decrease from injection 12 to separate its remaining critical pair without changing gradient slope. Monitor the neighboring pair for convergence; the last peak should still remain below 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 12 to raise its lone R 1.39 pair above 1.5 without the neighboring-pair convergence seen at 35 C. The last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes, potentially establishing another maximum-score method.

Trim injection 5's unused high-organic tail while preserving its starting fraction and gradient slope. The last peak previously eluted near organic fraction 0.57, so this shorter programmed gradient should retain full resolution and the maximum CRF.

Test a gradient slope of 0.080 organic fraction per minute, between the fully resolved 0.075 slope and injection 6's unsuccessful 0.090 slope. This probes whether retention can be shortened while preserving the maximum CRF, with injection 5 retained as the benchmark.

Test a slope of 0.065, between injection 14's marginally unresolved method and injection 16's fully resolved method. This should preserve full resolution while shortening retention relative to injection 16.

Reduce the slope from injection 13 to recover its limiting pair while preserving the stronger separation of the other central pair. This tests a potentially more robust maximum-score alternative, with the last peak expected to remain below 10 minutes.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 22 to bring its remaining R 1.41 pair above 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. This targets greater resolution margins at the maximum score; injection 5 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 23 to balance its two limiting resolutions and improve the minimum-resolution margin. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, preserving maximum CRF; injection 5 remains the fastest fully resolved method found.

Test one shallower step from injection 16 to strengthen its R 1.67 pair while checking that the other critical pair remains above 1.5 and the last peak stays below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already attained; injection 5 remains the fastest fully resolved method found.
